label: Preview: Robotics as Geometry
notes: This opening chapter, printed pages 1 through 10, frames the whole book. Robots are collections of rigid bodies, and every question about them becomes a question about spaces, maps, velocities, and forces. We preview the geometric language that unifies kinematics, dynamics, planning, and control across the entire course.

label: Mechanisms as Rigid Bodies
notes: A robot mechanism is a chain of rigid links joined by joints. We model it as a kinematic structure, not a drawing. Each joint, revolute or prismatic, contributes one or more degrees of freedom, and the end-effector frame is what a task actually cares about when reaching and grasping.

label: Configuration Space and DOF
notes: The configuration space collects every pose the mechanism can attain. For an open chain its dimension equals the number of joint variables, the degrees of freedom. Gruebler's formula counts them from links, joints, and constraints, and the space is often curved, like a torus, rather than flat Euclidean.

label: SO(3) and SE(3)
notes: Rotations form the Lie group SO(3) and rigid-body displacements form SE(3). These matrix groups, not raw angle triples, are the honest home of orientation and pose. Working in them avoids chart singularities like gimbal lock and gives a clean algebra for composing successive motions by matrix multiplication.

label: Twists: Velocity as Screw
notes: A spatial velocity is a twist, pairing angular and linear parts into one six-vector that lives in the Lie algebra se(3). By Chasles' theorem any rigid motion is a screw: rotation about an axis together with translation along it. Twists make velocity geometric rather than coordinate bound.

label: Wrenches: Force as Dual
notes: Forces and moments combine into a wrench, the dual object to a twist. The pairing of wrench with twist yields power, an invariant under change of frame. This duality between motion and force runs through statics, dynamics, and contact analysis across the entire book.

label: Product of Exponentials
notes: Forward kinematics maps joint angles to end-effector pose. The product of exponentials formula builds that pose by exponentiating each joint twist in turn and composing with the home configuration. It needs no intermediate link frames, only screw axes, making it geometric and remarkably easy to write down.

label: The Course Pipeline
notes: The book follows one pipeline: configuration and forward kinematics, then velocity kinematics and statics through the Jacobian, then dynamics, then trajectory generation and motion planning, and finally control. Each stage reuses twists, wrenches, and the Lie-group viewpoint, so mastering the geometry early pays off repeatedly later.

label: The Jacobian Hinge
notes: The Jacobian maps joint velocities to end-effector twists and, by its transpose, maps wrenches to joint torques. It is the hinge between kinematics, statics, and dynamics. Where it loses rank we meet singularities, configurations where instantaneous task motion collapses to a lower-dimensional set of directions.

label: Worked Invariants
notes: The notebook computes a planar-arm Jacobian rank, a rotation logarithm round trip, and a twist-wrench power pairing under a frame change. Each number names something that must stay invariant when the representation changes. Small residuals and stable ranks are exactly how we catch modeling mistakes early.

label: Recap and Outlook
notes: Robotics is organized around spaces, maps, velocities, forces, and feedback. The Lie groups SO(3) and SE(3), with twists and wrenches, supply one vocabulary reused in every later chapter. Name the representation and its invariant together, and the geometry stays inspectable throughout the rest of the course.
